case: A 34-year-old man comes to the physician because of swelling of his ankles for 2 months. Since childhood he has had episodes of burning pain in his hands and feet, and he sweats very little during exercise. His maternal grandfather required dialysis. Blood pressure is 138/86 mm Hg. Physical examination shows clusters of small dark red papules between the umbilicus and the knees. Urine protein excretion is 2.4 g/24 h (less than 0.15). Serum creatinine is 1.6 mg/dL (0.7 to 1.3). Leukocyte alpha-galactosidase A activity is markedly decreased. Kidney biopsy shows podocytes with vacuolated, foamy cytoplasm and segmental scarring of some glomerular tufts. Electron microscopy shows lamellated inclusions in podocytes. Diagnosis: Fabry disease nephropathy.

questions.stem: A timed urine collection is performed. His urine creatinine concentration is 96 mg/dL, urine flow is 1.25 mL/min, and plasma creatinine is 1.6 mg/dL. Inulin clearance measured on the same day is 62 mL/min. Which of the following best explains the difference between his creatinine clearance and his inulin clearance?
options: Binding of inulin to plasma albumin
approach: Calculate creatinine clearance: (96 mg/dL x 1.25 mL/min) / 1.6 mg/dL = 75 mL/min.
Compare it with inulin clearance, which equals GFR: 75 is above 62.
A clearance above GFR means the kidney adds the substance to urine by net secretion.
questions.why: Clearance is urine concentration times urine flow divided by plasma concentration. Inulin clearance equals GFR because inulin is freely filtered and not reabsorbed or secreted. Creatinine is freely filtered and also secreted by the proximal tubule through organic cation transporters, so its clearance runs above the true GFR. The gap widens as GFR falls, because secretion makes up a larger share of the creatinine excreted. A clearance below GFR means net reabsorption, and a clearance above GFR means net secretion.
whyNot: Net reabsorption would make creatinine clearance lower than GFR. His creatinine clearance (75 mL/min) is higher than his inulin clearance.
Inulin is freely filtered and is neither reabsorbed nor secreted. That is why its clearance equals GFR.
Correct.
Inulin is not protein bound, so all of it in plasma is filterable. Protein binding would lower its clearance, which is not the reason creatinine clearance is higher.

questions.stem: He and his wife, who is unaffected and has no family history of the disease, have two daughters and one son. Which of the following best describes which of his children inherited his disease-causing allele?
options: All of his daughters and none of his sons
Half of his sons and half of his daughters
All of his sons and none of his daughters
Half of his sons and none of his daughters
approach: Fabry disease is caused by mutations in GLA, an X-linked gene for alpha-galactosidase A.
An affected man has one X, which he passes to every daughter, and his Y, which he passes to every son.
So every daughter is a heterozygote and no son is affected.
questions.why: Fabry disease is an X-linked lysosomal storage disease. Deficient alpha-galactosidase A lets globotriaosylceramide (Gb3) build up in vascular endothelium, podocytes, tubular cells, nerves, and heart. This produces angiokeratomas, burning neuropathic pain, reduced sweating, and progressive proteinuric kidney failure. An affected father passes his X to all daughters, who are heterozygotes. Because of X inactivation, many heterozygous women develop symptoms, usually milder and later than in men.
whyNot: Correct.
This pattern fits autosomal dominant inheritance. The GLA gene is on the X chromosome, so a father passes it to his daughters only.
A father gives his Y chromosome to every son, never his X. Sons cannot inherit his X-linked allele.
A father never passes his X chromosome to a son, so no son can inherit the allele from him. Every daughter receives his X, so none of them can escape it.

questions.stem: The segmental scarring seen on his biopsy is a pattern of glomerular injury that also occurs in HIV infection, heroin use, sickle cell disease, and severe obesity. Loss of which of the following glomerular cells most directly leads to this pattern?
approach: Name the pattern: segmental sclerosis in some glomeruli is focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS).
Recall the common target in primary and secondary FSGS: the podocyte.
In Fabry disease, Gb3 storage injures podocytes, which detach and leave bare basement membrane that scars.
questions.why: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis starts with podocyte injury. When podocytes detach, the bare basement membrane sticks to Bowman capsule and the segment scars. Secondary causes include HIV (often the collapsing variant), heroin use, sickle cell disease, obesity, and loss of nephron mass. Storage of Gb3 in podocytes produces the same pattern in Fabry disease. FSGS causes nephrotic-range proteinuria, responds poorly to corticosteroids, and often progresses to kidney failure.
whyNot: Mesangial cells support the capillary loops and clear trapped material. Their expansion and proliferation mark IgA nephropathy and diabetic nodules, not podocyte-driven segmental sclerosis.
Endothelial injury drives thrombotic microangiopathy, as in hemolytic uremic syndrome, with fibrin thrombi in capillaries rather than segmental scarring.
Parietal cells line Bowman capsule. They can proliferate to form crescents in rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, but the starting lesion in this pattern is loss of visceral epithelial cells.
Correct.

questions.stem: The biopsy also shows Gb3 inclusions in a tubule segment that lies next to the vascular pole of its own glomerulus. Its cuboidal cells have no brush border, have a smaller cross-section than the adjacent proximal tubule, and contain a cluster of tightly packed nuclei facing the afferent arteriole. Which of the following segments is this?
approach: Use the brush border first: its absence rules out the proximal tubule.
Use the location: the distal tubule returns to the vascular pole of its own glomerulus, where its wall forms the macula densa.
The packed nuclei facing the afferent arteriole are the macula densa.
questions.why: The proximal tubule has tall cuboidal cells with a brush border and many mitochondria. Thin limbs are simple squamous. The distal tubule (the end of the thick ascending limb and the distal convoluted tubule) is cuboidal without a brush border. It returns to the vascular pole of its own glomerulus, where the end of the thick ascending limb forms the macula densa. Collecting ducts have principal and intercalated cells with clear cell borders. In Fabry disease, Gb3 collects prominently in distal tubule and loop of Henle epithelium as well as in podocytes.
whyNot: Proximal tubule cells are tall cuboidal cells with a prominent brush border and abundant mitochondria. This segment has no brush border.
Correct.
The thin limbs are lined by simple squamous epithelium and lie in the medulla, not at the vascular pole.
Collecting ducts are lined by principal and intercalated cells with distinct lateral borders. They run in medullary rays and do not contact the vascular pole of a glomerulus.

case: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of puffiness around his eyes for 1 week. It began a few days after an upper respiratory infection. His temperature is 36.9 °C (98.4 °F), pulse is 102/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 96/60 mm Hg. Physical examination shows periorbital edema, pitting edema of the legs, and scrotal swelling. Urinalysis shows 4+ protein and no blood. The urine protein to creatinine ratio is 7.5 mg/mg (less than 0.2). Serum albumin is 1.7 g/dL (3.5 to 5.5), total cholesterol is 360 mg/dL (less than 170), and creatinine is 0.3 mg/dL (0.2 to 0.4). Serum C3 is normal. Diagnosis: minimal change disease.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains his elevated serum cholesterol?
approach: Link the low serum albumin and low plasma oncotic pressure to the liver's response.
The liver raises synthesis of albumin and, with it, apolipoprotein B lipoproteins such as VLDL and LDL.
Reduced lipoprotein lipase activity also slows triglyceride-rich lipoprotein clearance.
questions.why: In nephrotic syndrome, the liver responds to low albumin and low oncotic pressure by making more protein, including apolipoprotein B lipoproteins, so VLDL and LDL rise. Catabolism also falls, partly because lipoprotein lipase activity is reduced. The other consequences of heavy proteinuria are edema from low oncotic pressure, a clotting tendency from urinary loss of antithrombin III, and infection from urinary loss of immunoglobulin.
whyNot: The kidney is not a route for cholesterol excretion. Cholesterol leaves the body mainly in bile.
Correct.
Hypoalbuminemia does not increase intestinal absorption. The lipid rise in nephrotic syndrome comes from the liver and reduced clearance.
Familial hypercholesterolemia causes lifelong high LDL from birth. His cholesterol rose together with heavy proteinuria and low albumin.

questions.stem: If a kidney biopsy were performed, which of the following findings would be most likely?
options: Subepithelial humps with granular IgG and C3
Linear IgG along the glomerular basement membrane
Mesangial IgA deposits with mesangial proliferation
Diffuse effacement of podocyte foot processes
approach: Recognize the classic child: nephrotic syndrome, no hematuria, normal blood pressure, normal C3.
Minimal change disease looks normal on light microscopy and immunofluorescence.
The only lesion is podocyte foot process effacement on electron microscopy.
questions.why: Minimal change disease is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in young children. Light microscopy and immunofluorescence are normal, and electron microscopy shows effacement of podocyte foot processes. Loss of the glomerular charge barrier gives selective albuminuria. Most children respond well to corticosteroids, so biopsy is usually reserved for those who do not. In adults it can be associated with Hodgkin lymphoma and with NSAID use.
whyNot: Subepithelial humps with granular IgG and C3 are the pattern of poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, which presents with hematuria, hypertension, and low C3.
Linear IgG marks anti-GBM disease, a nephritic process with hematuria and often lung hemorrhage.
Mesangial IgA marks IgA nephropathy, which usually presents with hematuria during or right after a mucosal infection.
Correct.

questions.stem: His edema develops as the kidneys retain sodium and water in about the same proportion as in plasma, and his serum sodium stays normal. Compared with before his illness, which of the following best describes the change in his body fluid compartments?
options: ECF increased, ICF unchanged, osmolality unchanged
ECF increased, ICF increased, osmolality decreased
ECF increased, ICF decreased, osmolality increased
ECF unchanged, ICF increased, osmolality decreased
approach: Classify the fluid gained: sodium and water in plasma proportion is an isotonic gain.
Isotonic fluid does not change osmolality, so no water shifts across cell membranes.
All of the gain stays in the ECF, much of it in the interstitium as edema.
questions.why: Water moves between ICF and ECF only when ECF osmolality changes. An isotonic gain adds volume to the ECF without changing its osmolality, so cell volume stays the same. A hypotonic gain lowers osmolality, and water enters cells, so both compartments expand. A hypertonic gain raises osmolality and pulls water out of cells. In nephrotic syndrome the extra ECF collects in the interstitium because low plasma oncotic pressure favors filtration out of capillaries.
whyNot: Correct.
This is a hypotonic gain, such as retained free water. His serum sodium is normal, so osmolality has not fallen.
This is a hypertonic gain, such as hypertonic saline. Water would leave cells, and serum sodium would rise.
Water alone would spread into both compartments. Retained isotonic fluid stays in the extracellular space.

questions.stem: In his disease, immunofluorescence shows no immunoglobulin or complement in the glomeruli. A rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis that also shows few or no immune deposits on immunofluorescence is most characteristic of which of the following?
approach: Sort immune glomerular injury by immunofluorescence pattern: linear, granular, or pauci-immune.
Linear IgG is anti-GBM (type II). Granular deposits are immune complexes (type III).
Pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis is ANCA-associated vasculitis, such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis.
questions.why: Immune glomerular injury falls into three groups. Type II hypersensitivity is anti-GBM disease, with linear IgG and, in Goodpasture syndrome, lung hemorrhage. Type III is immune complex disease with granular deposits, as in poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis and lupus. The third group is pauci-immune disease, in which ANCA-activated neutrophils injure the capillaries and immunofluorescence shows little or no immunoglobulin. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (PR3-ANCA) and microscopic polyangiitis (MPO-ANCA) are examples. Minimal change disease also lacks deposits, but it is a podocyte disease, not an inflammatory glomerulonephritis.
whyNot: Anti-GBM disease is type II hypersensitivity, with antibodies to the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen. It shows bright linear IgG on immunofluorescence.
This is type III immune complex disease with granular IgG and C3 deposits.
Correct.
Lupus nephritis is type III immune complex disease with granular deposits of many immunoglobulins and complement, a full-house pattern.

case: A 38-year-old man comes to the physician because of foamy urine and swelling of his legs for 6 weeks. Chronic hepatitis B was diagnosed 10 years ago, and he has not been treated. Blood pressure is 128/80 mm Hg. Physical examination shows pitting edema to the knees. Urine protein excretion is 6.8 g/24 h (less than 0.15). Serum albumin is 2.2 g/dL (3.5 to 5.5), total cholesterol is 320 mg/dL (less than 200), and creatinine is 1.0 mg/dL (0.7 to 1.3). HBsAg and HBeAg are positive. Serum anti-phospholipase A2 receptor (anti-PLA2R) antibody is negative. Kidney biopsy shows diffusely thickened glomerular capillary walls without cell proliferation, and immunofluorescence shows granular IgG and C3 along the capillary walls. Diagnosis: hepatitis B associated membranous nephropathy.

questions.stem: During his hospital stay he drinks large volumes of water, and much of it is retained. His serum sodium falls from 138 mEq/L to 127 mEq/L (136 to 145). Compared with admission, which of the following best describes the change in his body fluid compartments?
options: ECF increased, ICF unchanged, osmolality unchanged
ECF increased, ICF decreased, osmolality increased
ECF decreased, ICF increased, osmolality decreased
ECF increased, ICF increased, osmolality decreased
approach: Classify the change: retained free water is a hypotonic gain.
Lower ECF osmolality draws water into cells until osmolality is equal on both sides.
Both compartments enlarge, and osmolality in both falls.
questions.why: Free water distributes across both compartments in proportion to their size, about two thirds into cells. A hypotonic gain therefore expands both ECF and ICF and lowers osmolality everywhere, which shows up as a lower serum sodium. In the brain, this cell swelling explains the confusion and seizures of severe acute hyponatremia. An isotonic gain stays in the ECF, and a hypertonic gain shrinks cells.
whyNot: This is an isotonic gain, such as normal saline. His falling serum sodium shows that osmolality has dropped.
This is a hypertonic gain. Serum sodium would rise, and water would move out of cells.
This pattern follows loss of salt in excess of water, as with heavy sweating replaced by water alone. He has gained water, so ECF volume rises.
Correct.

questions.stem: Electron microscopy of his biopsy is most likely to show which of the following?
options: Subendothelial deposits with basement membrane duplication
Subepithelial deposits between basement membrane spikes
Mesangial deposits with mesangial cell proliferation
Foot process effacement without immune deposits
approach: Nephrotic syndrome in an adult with thick capillary walls, no proliferation, and granular IgG is membranous nephropathy.
In membranous nephropathy, immune complexes form on the outer (subepithelial) side of the basement membrane.
New basement membrane grows between the deposits, giving spikes on silver stain and a spike-and-dome look.
questions.why: Membranous nephropathy is a common cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults. Immune complexes sit in the subepithelial space, and the basement membrane grows up around them, producing spikes on silver stain. Most primary cases are caused by autoantibodies to the podocyte phospholipase A2 receptor (anti-PLA2R). Secondary causes include lupus, hepatitis B, solid tumors, and drugs such as NSAIDs. His negative anti-PLA2R and active hepatitis B point to a secondary form.
whyNot: Subendothelial deposits with a split, tram-track basement membrane mark membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis. Hepatitis C is a classic cause of that pattern.
Correct.
Mesangial deposits with proliferation mark IgA nephropathy. His biopsy shows thick capillary walls without proliferation.
Effacement without deposits is minimal change disease. His immunofluorescence shows granular IgG and C3, so deposits are present.

questions.stem: His 7-year-old daughter is tested. Her results show negative HBsAg, negative anti-HBc, and positive anti-HBs. Which of the following best explains these results?
options: Recovery from a past natural infection
approach: Note that anti-HBs is present but anti-HBc is absent.
The vaccine contains only recombinant surface antigen, so it induces anti-HBs and never anti-HBc.
Anti-HBs alone therefore means immunity from vaccination.
questions.why: The hepatitis B vaccine is made of recombinant HBsAg. It induces neutralizing anti-HBs antibodies that protect against infection. Because the vaccine has no core antigen, vaccinated people are anti-HBc negative. Natural infection produces anti-HBc, and recovery adds anti-HBs. Vaccination prevents chronic hepatitis B and so prevents its immune complex complications, including membranous nephropathy.
whyNot: Natural infection exposes the immune system to the core antigen, so anti-HBc would be positive along with anti-HBs.
In the window period HBsAg has cleared but anti-HBs is not yet detectable, and IgM anti-HBc is positive. She has anti-HBs and no anti-HBc.
Correct.
A carrier has persistent HBsAg and positive anti-HBc. Her HBsAg is negative.

questions.stem: Urine sediment shows tubular cells filled with refractile droplets and casts that show a Maltese cross pattern under polarized light. Which of the following lipids is responsible for this birefringence?
approach: Link heavy proteinuria to leakage of lipoproteins across the damaged glomerular barrier.
Tubular cells take up the filtered lipid, becoming oval fat bodies, and shed into fatty casts.
The droplets that polarize as a Maltese cross are cholesteryl esters.
questions.why: In nephrotic syndrome, lipoproteins leak through the injured glomerular barrier. Tubular cells absorb the lipid and are shed as oval fat bodies, or they form fatty casts. Under polarized light, cholesteryl ester droplets are birefringent and show a Maltese cross. This lipiduria accompanies the hyperlipidemia of nephrotic syndrome, and fatty casts point to a nephrotic process.
whyNot: Correct.
Triglycerides stain with fat stains but are not birefringent under polarized light.
Free fatty acids travel bound to albumin and do not form the anisotropic droplets that make a Maltese cross.
Bile acids are not part of the lipid droplets in urine sediment. Bile pigments color urine in cholestasis but do not form these droplets.

dx: AL amyloidosis with nephrotic syndrome and renal vein thrombosis
case: A 63-year-old man comes to the physician because of progressive leg swelling and fatigue for 3 months. Physical examination shows an enlarged tongue with indentations from his teeth and pitting edema to the thighs. Urine protein excretion is 9.5 g/24 h (less than 0.15). Serum albumin is 1.8 g/dL (3.5 to 5.5). The serum free kappa to lambda light chain ratio is 0.08 (0.26 to 1.65), and bone marrow biopsy shows 9% clonal lambda plasma cells. A percutaneous kidney biopsy shows glomeruli filled with amorphous pink extracellular material. Three weeks later he develops sudden left flank pain and gross hematuria, and CT shows a thrombus in the left renal vein. Diagnosis: AL amyloidosis with nephrotic syndrome complicated by left renal vein thrombosis.

questions.stem: Two days after the flank pain begins, he notices a new soft mass of dilated veins in the left side of his scrotum. Which of the following anatomic features best explains why this developed on the left side?
options: The left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein
The left testicular vein drains into the inferior vena cava
The left renal vein passes behind the abdominal aorta
The left testicular artery arises from the left renal artery
approach: Identify the scrotal mass of dilated veins as a varicocele.
Recall venous drainage: left testicular vein to left renal vein, right testicular vein to the IVC.
Blockage of the left renal vein raises pressure in the left testicular vein and pampiniform plexus.
questions.why: The left renal vein is long. It crosses in front of the aorta just below the origin of the superior mesenteric artery, where it can be compressed (nutcracker phenomenon). It receives the left testicular (or ovarian) vein and the left suprarenal vein. Thrombosis of the left renal vein, or invasion by renal cell carcinoma, raises pressure in the left testicular vein and causes a new left varicocele. The right testicular vein drains straight into the IVC, so this does not happen on the right.
whyNot: Correct.
This describes the right testicular vein. On the left, the testicular vein drains into the left renal vein, so a renal vein clot backs up into it.
The left renal vein normally crosses in front of the aorta, just below the superior mesenteric artery. A retroaortic vein is an uncommon variant.
The testicular arteries arise from the aorta. Arterial anatomy would not cause venous dilation.

questions.stem: Congo red stain of the kidney biopsy shows apple-green birefringence under polarized light. Which of the following proteins most likely forms these deposits?
options: Serum amyloid A acute phase protein
approach: Apple-green birefringence with Congo red confirms amyloid, a beta-pleated sheet protein.
Use the clues to the source: abnormal light chain ratio and clonal plasma cells.
Misfolded light chains from the plasma cell clone form AL amyloid.
questions.why: Amyloid is misfolded protein arranged in beta-pleated sheets. It binds Congo red and shows apple-green birefringence under polarized light. AL amyloid comes from monoclonal light chains, most often lambda, made by a plasma cell clone. AA amyloid comes from serum amyloid A in chronic inflammation. In the kidney, amyloid fills the mesangium and capillary walls and disrupts the filtration barrier, which causes heavy proteinuria. An enlarged tongue is a classic sign of AL amyloidosis.
whyNot: AA amyloid comes from serum amyloid A, an acute phase protein made in chronic inflammation such as rheumatoid arthritis or chronic infection. He has a clonal plasma cell disorder.
Transthyretin amyloid usually affects the heart and nerves in older adults or in hereditary forms, and does not explain his abnormal light chain ratio.
Correct.
Beta-2 microglobulin amyloid forms in patients on long-term dialysis and deposits in joints and the carpal tunnel.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings in the left kidney is most likely on his CT scan?
approach: Venous outflow is blocked while arterial inflow continues.
Blood and fluid back up into the kidney, causing congestion, swelling, flank pain, and hematuria.
Nephrotic syndrome is a leading cause, because urinary loss of antithrombin III makes blood hypercoagulable.
questions.why: Renal vein thrombosis causes flank pain, hematuria, and an enlarged, congested kidney. The main causes are nephrotic syndrome, especially membranous nephropathy, renal cell carcinoma growing into the vein, and dehydration in infants. In nephrotic syndrome, antithrombin III is small enough to be lost in urine, while the liver makes more clotting factors such as fibrinogen. Both shifts favor thrombosis.
whyNot: Small, scarred kidneys reflect chronic damage such as chronic pyelonephritis or vascular disease. Acute venous blockage makes the kidney swell.
Correct.
A wedge-shaped infarct follows blockage of an artery branch, usually by an embolus. His clot is in the vein.
A dilated collecting system means urinary obstruction, such as a stone or tumor, not venous thrombosis.

questions.stem: A CT scan obtained after his kidney biopsy showed a hematoma surrounding the kidney within the perirenal fat. Which of the following structures limited the spread of this hematoma?
approach: List the coverings from inside out: fibrous capsule, perirenal fat, renal fascia, pararenal fat.
Blood in the perirenal fat lies outside the capsule but inside the renal fascia.
So the renal fascia contains a perinephric hematoma.
questions.why: The kidney is wrapped in layers. The fibrous capsule sits on the kidney surface. Around it is perirenal fat, enclosed by the renal (Gerota) fascia, which also encloses the adrenal gland. Outside the fascia is pararenal fat. A perinephric hematoma or abscess stays within the renal fascia. At the hilum, structures run from front to back as renal vein, renal artery, and renal pelvis.
whyNot: The fibrous capsule clings to the kidney surface. Blood under it forms a thin subcapsular hematoma that hugs the kidney, not one within the perirenal fat.
The peritoneum lies in front of the renal fascia and pararenal fat. It would limit blood only after the blood had escaped the renal fascia.
Transversalis fascia lines the inner abdominal wall. It lies outside the pararenal fat and does not enclose the perirenal space.
Correct.

dx: Myeloma cast nephropathy with acquired Fanconi syndrome
case: A 67-year-old woman comes to the physician because of low back pain and fatigue for 4 months. Laboratory studies show hemoglobin 9.2 g/dL (12 to 16), serum calcium 11.6 mg/dL (8.5 to 10.5), creatinine 2.9 mg/dL (0.6 to 1.1), fasting plasma glucose 92 mg/dL (70 to 99), phosphate 1.9 mg/dL (2.5 to 4.5), bicarbonate 17 mEq/L (22 to 28), and chloride 112 mEq/L (98 to 106). Urinalysis shows 2+ glucose. Urine studies show generalized aminoaciduria and large amounts of free kappa light chains. Bone marrow biopsy shows 35% clonal kappa plasma cells. Kidney biopsy shows tubules plugged with dense, fractured casts surrounded by multinucleated giant cells. Diagnosis: multiple myeloma cast nephropathy with acquired Fanconi syndrome.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the glucose in her urine?
options: Plasma glucose above the renal threshold
approach: Note glucosuria with a normal plasma glucose, so the filtered load is normal.
Glucose is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule by SGLT2 and SGLT1 with a transport maximum.
Injury to proximal cells lowers that transport maximum, so normal filtered glucose spills into urine.
questions.why: Filtered glucose is reclaimed almost entirely in the proximal tubule. SGLT2 in the early proximal tubule does most of the work, using the sodium gradient made by the basolateral Na+/K+ ATPase. Because the carriers can be saturated, glucose appears in urine when plasma glucose exceeds about 200 mg/dL, as in uncontrolled diabetes, and the extra solute causes an osmotic diuresis. Here the plasma glucose is normal, so the glucosuria must come from damaged proximal cells with a lower transport maximum.
whyNot: The renal threshold is about 200 mg/dL. Her plasma glucose is 92 mg/dL, so filtered glucose is well within normal reabsorptive capacity.
Almost all filtered glucose is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule. The distal nephron has little capacity to reclaim it.
Correct.
The kidney does not secrete glucose. Glucose appears in urine only when filtered glucose escapes proximal reabsorption.

questions.stem: Filtered free light chains are normally taken up by endocytosis and broken down in the tubule segment whose failure explains her glucosuria, aminoaciduria, and phosphaturia. Which of the following best describes the epithelium of that segment?
options: Simple squamous cells with few organelles and no brush border
Cuboidal cells with lateral interdigitations but no brush border
Principal cells mixed with acid-secreting intercalated cells
Cuboidal cells with a brush border and many mitochondria
approach: Glucosuria, aminoaciduria, phosphaturia, and bicarbonate loss point to the proximal tubule.
The proximal tubule reclaims filtered small proteins, including light chains, by endocytosis.
Its cells are cuboidal with a brush border for surface area and many mitochondria for active transport.
questions.why: Proximal tubule cells have a dense microvillous brush border, a busy endocytic and lysosomal system, and many basal mitochondria that power Na+/K+ ATPase. They reclaim filtered low molecular weight proteins such as light chains. When light chains flood these cells, lysosomal handling fails and transport is impaired, causing Fanconi syndrome. The same high energy demand makes the proximal tubule very sensitive to ischemia.
whyNot: This describes the thin limbs of the loop of Henle, which do little active transport or protein uptake.
This describes the distal tubule. It lacks the brush border and endocytic machinery used to reclaim filtered proteins.
These line the collecting duct, where sodium, potassium, water, and acid are fine-tuned. They do not reclaim filtered proteins.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following conditions also causes this pattern of tubular dysfunction?
approach: Name her pattern: glucosuria with normal plasma glucose, aminoaciduria, phosphaturia, and bicarbonate wasting is Fanconi syndrome.
Fanconi syndrome is generalized proximal tubule failure.
Its causes include cystinosis, Wilson disease, multiple myeloma, and some drugs and heavy metals.
questions.why: Fanconi syndrome is generalized failure of proximal tubule reabsorption. Glucose, amino acids, phosphate, bicarbonate, and uric acid are lost in urine. Loss of bicarbonate causes a proximal (type 2) renal tubular acidosis, and loss of phosphate causes rickets or osteomalacia. In children, cystinosis is the classic inherited cause. Acquired causes include multiple myeloma light chains, Wilson disease (copper injury), heavy metals such as lead, and drugs such as tenofovir and expired tetracycline.
whyNot: Correct.
Lithium blocks ADH action in the collecting duct, causing dilute polyuria. It does not cause glucosuria or aminoaciduria.
Liddle syndrome is overactivity of the collecting duct sodium channel ENaC, causing hypertension, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis.
Bartter syndrome is a defect in thick ascending limb salt transport. It causes hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, not proximal wasting of glucose and amino acids.

questions.stem: Her serum bicarbonate is 17 mEq/L, and her urine pH is 5.4. When an infusion of sodium bicarbonate raises her serum bicarbonate to 22 mEq/L, her urine pH rises to 7.6 and more than 15% of filtered bicarbonate appears in the urine. Which of the following transport functions is most likely impaired?
approach: Normally the proximal tubule reclaims about 80% of filtered bicarbonate.
Na+/H+ exchange secretes H+, which joins filtered bicarbonate; carbonic anhydrase turns it into CO2 and water, which enter the cell and regenerate bicarbonate.
When this fails, bicarbonate spills into urine whenever serum bicarbonate is above a new, lower threshold, as during the infusion.
questions.why: In the proximal tubule, the apical Na+/H+ exchanger secretes H+. Brush border carbonic anhydrase converts H+ and filtered bicarbonate to CO2 and water, which diffuse into the cell. Inside, carbonic anhydrase rebuilds bicarbonate, which leaves across the basolateral membrane with sodium. The kidney also makes new bicarbonate by excreting H+ as titratable acid (mainly phosphate) and as ammonium made from glutamine in the proximal tubule. Proximal (type 2) RTA lowers the threshold for bicarbonate reabsorption, causing a normal anion gap acidosis. Once serum bicarbonate falls low enough, the distal nephron can still acidify the urine.
whyNot: Defective distal H+ secretion is distal (type 1) RTA. It does not cause glucosuria or aminoaciduria.
Correct.
Aldosterone deficiency or resistance causes type 4 RTA with hyperkalemia, and urine can still be acidified.
Loss of NKCC2 transport causes salt wasting with hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, as with loop diuretics or Bartter syndrome.

dx: Chronic kidney disease from diabetes and hypertension with renal osteodystrophy
case: A 58-year-old woman with a 20-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension comes to the physician because of fatigue, itching, and aching bones for 6 months. Blood pressure is 162/96 mm Hg. Laboratory studies show hemoglobin 9.1 g/dL (12 to 16), urea nitrogen 68 mg/dL (7 to 20), creatinine 3.4 mg/dL (0.6 to 1.1), potassium 5.6 mEq/L (3.5 to 5.0), bicarbonate 17 mEq/L (22 to 28), calcium 7.9 mg/dL (8.5 to 10.5), phosphate 6.3 mg/dL (2.5 to 4.5), and parathyroid hormone 420 pg/mL (10 to 65). Estimated GFR is 16 mL/min/1.73 m2. Ultrasound shows two small, echogenic kidneys. Diagnosis: chronic kidney disease due to diabetic and hypertensive nephropathy, with renal osteodystrophy.

questions.stem: Which of the following most directly contributes to her low serum calcium?
approach: Note the pattern: low calcium, high phosphate, high PTH in advanced CKD.
The proximal tubule makes calcitriol through 1-alpha-hydroxylase, and lost nephron mass plus high phosphate and FGF23 reduce this.
Low calcitriol cuts intestinal calcium absorption, and retained phosphate binds calcium, so calcium falls and PTH rises.
questions.why: Proximal tubule 1-alpha-hydroxylase converts 25-hydroxyvitamin D to calcitriol. PTH and low phosphate stimulate it, and high phosphate and FGF23 suppress it. In CKD, nephron loss and phosphate retention reduce calcitriol, so calcium falls and PTH rises (secondary hyperparathyroidism). The result is renal osteodystrophy. Primary hyperparathyroidism gives high calcium, low phosphate, and high PTH. Vitamin D deficiency gives low or normal calcium, low phosphate, and high PTH. Low magnesium blocks PTH release and action, so hypocalcemia does not correct until magnesium is replaced.
whyNot: The liver adds the 25-hydroxyl group, and that step is usually preserved in kidney disease. The step that fails is in the kidney.
Correct.
Her PTH is high, not suppressed. Low calcium, high phosphate, and low calcitriol all drive PTH up.
With a GFR of 16 mL/min/1.73 m2, less calcium is filtered. Urinary calcium loss is not what lowers her serum calcium.

questions.stem: She reports getting up three times each night to urinate. After an overnight water restriction, her urine osmolality is 300 mOsm/kg (normal response greater than 600 after restriction), and it does not rise after desmopressin. Which of the following best explains her inability to concentrate urine?
options: Deficient ADH release from the posterior pituitary
Excess ADH secretion with free water retention
Excess water intake suppressing ADH release
approach: Urine that cannot rise above plasma osmolality despite restriction and desmopressin points to a kidney problem, not an ADH problem.
ADH can concentrate urine only as far as the medullary interstitium is hypertonic.
In CKD, fewer nephrons each carry a high solute load and medullary structure is damaged, so the countercurrent gradient is lost.
questions.why: The thick ascending limb pumps NaCl into the medulla without water, and countercurrent flow in the loop multiplies this into a gradient up to about 1200 mOsm/kg. ADH inserts aquaporin-2 into collecting duct cells so water follows that gradient. In advanced CKD, each remaining nephron carries a high solute load and medullary structure is damaged. The gradient is lost, and urine stays near plasma osmolality (isosthenuria) whatever the ADH level. Central diabetes insipidus responds to desmopressin, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus does not, SIADH gives concentrated urine with low serum sodium, and primary polydipsia concentrates with water restriction.
whyNot: Correct.
In central diabetes insipidus, urine osmolality rises clearly after desmopressin. Hers does not change.
Excess ADH, as in SIADH, makes urine inappropriately concentrated. Her urine stays dilute.
In primary polydipsia, urine concentrates after water restriction. Her urine stays at about plasma osmolality.

questions.stem: She takes extra doses of oxycodone for bone pain and is brought to the emergency department because she is drowsy. Arterial blood gas analysis on room air shows pH 7.25, PaCO2 40 mm Hg, and bicarbonate 17 mEq/L. Which of the following best describes her acid-base status?
options: Metabolic acidosis with appropriate respiratory compensation
Metabolic acidosis with concurrent respiratory alkalosis
Respiratory acidosis with appropriate renal compensation
Metabolic acidosis with concurrent respiratory acidosis
approach: pH below 7.35 with low bicarbonate is a primary metabolic acidosis.
Apply Winters formula: expected PaCO2 = 1.5 x 17 + 8 = 33.5, plus or minus 2.
Her PaCO2 of 40 mm Hg is higher than expected, so she also has a respiratory acidosis from opioid hypoventilation.
questions.why: In metabolic acidosis the lungs normally lower PaCO2 to the value predicted by Winters formula (1.5 x bicarbonate + 8, plus or minus 2). A PaCO2 above that range means a second process, respiratory acidosis, is present. Here, opioids depress her breathing on top of the metabolic acidosis of CKD. A PaCO2 below the range would mean an added respiratory alkalosis. A normal PaCO2 in a patient with low bicarbonate is a warning sign of a mixed disorder.
whyNot: Winters formula predicts a PaCO2 of 1.5 x 17 + 8 = 33.5, plus or minus 2. Her PaCO2 of 40 mm Hg is too high to be compensation alone.
A concurrent respiratory alkalosis would push PaCO2 below the expected range of about 31.5 to 35.5 mm Hg. Hers is above it.
Renal compensation for respiratory acidosis raises bicarbonate. Her bicarbonate is low, so the main process is metabolic acidosis.
Correct.

questions.stem: One month later she has bleeding gums and large bruises after minor bumps. Platelet count is 210,000/mm3 (150,000 to 400,000), and prothrombin time and partial thromboplastin time are normal. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her bleeding?
approach: Mucocutaneous bleeding with normal platelet count, PT, and PTT points to a problem with platelet function.
Retained uremic toxins impair platelet adhesion and aggregation.
This uremic platelet dysfunction is a complication of advanced CKD.
questions.why: Diabetes and hypertension are the leading causes of CKD. As GFR falls, uremic toxins build up and cause pericarditis, encephalopathy, itching, and platelet dysfunction with a prolonged bleeding time. Other consequences include hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, volume overload, hypertension, anemia from low erythropoietin, and renal osteodystrophy. Dialysis improves uremic platelet dysfunction, and desmopressin helps short term by releasing von Willebrand factor.
whyNot: Vitamin K deficiency lowers factors II, VII, IX, and X and prolongs the prothrombin time. Her PT is normal.
Her platelet count is normal, so platelet number is not the problem.
Correct.
A factor VIII inhibitor prolongs the partial thromboplastin time. Her PTT is normal.

dx: Prerenal acute kidney injury from persistent vomiting
case: A 45-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of repeated vomiting of undigested food for 5 days. She has a long history of peptic ulcer disease, and endoscopy later shows pyloric channel narrowing. Her temperature is 36.8 °C (98.2 °F), pulse is 114/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 94/58 mm Hg. Mucous membranes are dry. Laboratory studies show sodium 134 mEq/L (136 to 145), potassium 2.8 mEq/L (3.5 to 5.0), chloride 84 mEq/L (98 to 106), bicarbonate 36 mEq/L (22 to 28), urea nitrogen 46 mg/dL (7 to 20), and creatinine 2.0 mg/dL (0.6 to 1.1); her creatinine was 0.8 mg/dL a year ago. Arterial pH is 7.52. Urine sodium is 9 mEq/L (less than 20 in prerenal states), and the fractional excretion of sodium is 0.4% (less than 1% in prerenal states). Diagnosis: prerenal acute kidney injury due to volume depletion from vomiting.

questions.stem: An ECG is obtained. Which of the following findings is most likely?
approach: Note her potassium of 2.8 mEq/L and her alkalemia.
Alkalosis moves potassium into cells, and volume-driven aldosterone and high distal bicarbonate delivery increase urinary potassium loss.
Hypokalemia slows repolarization and produces U waves and flattened T waves.
questions.why: Potassium moves into cells with insulin, beta-adrenergic stimulation, and alkalosis. It moves out with acidosis, cell lysis, insulin deficiency, and hyperosmolality. In vomiting, the larger potassium loss is through the kidney, driven by aldosterone and by bicarbonate reaching the distal nephron, and alkalosis shifts more into cells. Hypokalemia causes flattened T waves, ST depression, and U waves, with a risk of arrhythmia. Hyperkalemia causes peaked T waves and then QRS widening.
whyNot: Peaked T waves are an early sign of hyperkalemia. Her potassium is low.
QRS widening appears in more severe hyperkalemia, as conduction slows.
A short QT is typical of hypercalcemia. It is not a feature of hypokalemia.
Correct.

questions.stem: Her urine pH is 5.5 despite her arterial pH of 7.52. Which of the following best explains the acidic urine?
options: Loss of bicarbonate-rich fluid in the vomitus
Decreased renal ammonium production from hypokalemia
approach: Vomiting removes HCl, which raises bicarbonate and lowers chloride (the generation phase).
Volume depletion activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and makes the kidney hold on to sodium (the maintenance phase).
With little chloride to reabsorb with sodium, sodium is reclaimed in exchange for H+ and K+, so the urine becomes acidic.
questions.why: Each H+ lost in vomitus leaves a new bicarbonate in blood. Normally the kidney would excrete the extra bicarbonate, but volume depletion prevents this. Angiotensin II increases proximal Na+/H+ exchange and bicarbonate reabsorption. Aldosterone drives distal H+ and K+ secretion, so urine is acidic even though blood is alkaline (paradoxical aciduria). Low chloride limits sodium reabsorption with chloride. Giving normal saline restores volume and chloride and lets the kidney excrete the extra bicarbonate.
whyNot: Vomitus is rich in hydrochloric acid, not bicarbonate. Losing it raises serum bicarbonate.
Hypokalemia increases proximal ammonium production. It does not lower acid excretion.
Correct.
Respiratory compensation raises PaCO2 to bring blood pH down. It does not make the urine acidic.

questions.stem: Her plasma renin activity is markedly increased. Which of the following cells release renin into her circulation?
options: Tubular epithelial cells forming the macula densa plaque
Modified smooth muscle cells in the afferent arteriole
Extraglomerular mesangial cells between the two arterioles
Endothelial cells lining the efferent arteriole lumen
approach: Volume depletion lowers afferent arteriole stretch, increases renal sympathetic activity, and lowers NaCl delivery to the macula densa.
All three signals converge on the juxtaglomerular apparatus.
Renin is stored and released by juxtaglomerular cells, which are modified smooth muscle cells in the afferent arteriole wall.
questions.why: The juxtaglomerular apparatus has three parts. Juxtaglomerular cells are modified, granule-containing smooth muscle cells in the afferent arteriole that secrete renin. The macula densa is a plaque of cells at the end of the thick ascending limb that senses NaCl. Extraglomerular mesangial cells sit between the two arterioles. Renin release rises with low afferent pressure, beta-1 sympathetic stimulation, and low macula densa NaCl. Intraglomerular mesangial cells support the capillary tuft and clear trapped material by phagocytosis.
whyNot: Macula densa cells sense NaCl delivery and signal renin release, but they do not secrete renin themselves.
Correct.
Extraglomerular mesangial (lacis) cells lie between the arterioles and may relay signals, but they do not secrete renin.
The efferent arteriole is a site of angiotensin II action, not of renin secretion.

questions.stem: Her mean arterial pressure is about 70 mm Hg. Before her blood pressure fell this low, falling NaCl delivery to the macula densa had triggered a feedback response that helped hold her GFR steady. Which of the following arteriolar changes is the direct result of this feedback?
approach: Low perfusion lowers GFR, so less NaCl reaches the macula densa.
The macula densa reduces adenosine signaling, and the afferent arteriole dilates.
Dilation raises glomerular capillary pressure and supports GFR, but only within the autoregulatory range of mean pressure (about 80 to 180 mm Hg).
questions.why: Renal autoregulation keeps blood flow and GFR fairly constant over a mean arterial pressure of about 80 to 180 mm Hg. In the myogenic response, the afferent arteriole constricts when stretched and relaxes when pressure falls. In tubuloglomerular feedback, the macula densa senses NaCl. High NaCl causes afferent constriction, largely through adenosine, and low NaCl causes afferent dilation and renin release. Her mean pressure of about 70 mm Hg is below the autoregulatory range, so GFR falls and prerenal azotemia develops.
whyNot: Correct.
Constriction is the response to high NaCl delivery, which signals that GFR is too high.
Efferent dilation would lower glomerular pressure and GFR. Angiotensin II acts the other way, constricting the efferent arteriole.
Tubuloglomerular feedback acts on the afferent arteriole of each nephron, not on the main renal artery.

dx: Ischemic acute tubular necrosis after hemorrhagic shock
case: A 52-year-old man undergoes emergency surgery for a bleeding duodenal ulcer. Before transfusion, his blood pressure stayed near 70/40 mm Hg for about 90 minutes. Over the next 2 days, his urine output is 300 mL/day. His serum creatinine rises from 0.9 mg/dL to 4.1 mg/dL (0.7 to 1.3). Urine sodium is 58 mEq/L, the fractional excretion of sodium is 4% (less than 1% in prerenal states), and urine osmolality is 310 mOsm/kg. Urine microscopy shows many muddy brown granular casts and renal tubular epithelial cells. Diagnosis: ischemic acute tubular necrosis.

questions.stem: The outer medulla of his kidneys is especially vulnerable to this injury. Which of the following features of the renal circulation best explains this vulnerability?
options: Slow vasa recta flow with countercurrent oxygen exchange
High-pressure glomerular capillaries in the cortex
Efferent arterioles supplying cortical peritubular capillaries
Arcuate arteries running along the corticomedullary border
approach: The medulla gets only a small share of renal blood flow, through the vasa recta.
The vasa recta are arranged as a countercurrent loop, so oxygen diffuses from descending to ascending vessels and bypasses the deep medulla.
Slow flow and oxygen shunting keep medullary oxygen tension low, while thick ascending limb cells there use a lot of oxygen.
questions.why: The vasa recta carry a small, slow flow through the medulla. This protects the medullary osmotic gradient, because slow countercurrent flow lets solutes exchange without being washed out. The same arrangement shunts oxygen from descending to ascending vessels, so medullary tissue lives at a low oxygen tension. The straight proximal tubule and the medullary thick ascending limb, both active transporters, are the first to die when perfusion falls. Low medullary oxygen also explains papillary necrosis and sickling of red cells in the vasa recta in sickle cell disease and trait.
whyNot: Correct.
Glomerular capillaries are part of the cortex, which receives most of renal blood flow and has a higher oxygen tension than the medulla.
Cortical peritubular capillaries carry a high flow of blood. The oxygen supply problem is in the medulla.
Arcuate arteries are large distributing vessels. They do not create a low-oxygen zone.

questions.stem: On day 3 his serum potassium is 6.7 mEq/L (3.5 to 5.0) and his arterial pH is 7.22. Which of the following mechanisms links his acidemia to his rising potassium?
options: Increased Na+/K+ ATPase activity in muscle cells
Movement of K+ out of cells as H+ moves in
Increased insulin release from pancreatic beta cells
approach: Identify the shift factor: acidemia.
Cells buffer extra H+ by taking it up, and K+ leaves to keep electrical balance.
This shift adds to the reduced renal potassium excretion of oliguric acute tubular necrosis.
questions.why: In acidemia, H+ enters cells to be buffered, and K+ leaves to keep the charge balance, so serum potassium rises. This effect is strongest in mineral (normal anion gap) acidosis. Cell lysis, insulin deficiency, beta blockade, and hyperosmolality also move potassium out of cells. Insulin, beta-2 stimulation, and alkalosis move it in. In oliguric acute tubular necrosis, low distal flow and tubular damage also reduce potassium excretion. Hyperkalemia first causes peaked T waves, then a wide QRS and arrhythmias.
whyNot: Increased pump activity, as with insulin or beta-2 agonists, moves potassium into cells and lowers serum potassium.
Correct.
More distal secretion would lower serum potassium. His failing tubules secrete less potassium.
Insulin drives potassium into cells. Insulin deficiency, not excess, moves potassium out.

questions.stem: As he recovers, his serum magnesium is 1.3 mg/dL (1.7 to 2.2) with inappropriately high urinary magnesium losses. In the normal kidney, paracellular reabsorption of Mg2+ in the thick ascending limb depends most directly on which of the following?
options: Solvent drag from transcellular water reabsorption
Basolateral Na+/Ca2+ exchange in tubular cells
A lumen-positive voltage from K+ recycling
approach: The thick ascending limb takes up Na+, K+, and 2 Cl- through NKCC2.
K+ leaks back into the lumen through ROMK channels, making the lumen positive.
This positive voltage pushes Mg2+ and Ca2+ between cells through tight junctions.
questions.why: The thick ascending limb reabsorbs about 25% of filtered sodium through apical NKCC2, and it is impermeable to water, which dilutes the tubular fluid. Potassium recycled through ROMK makes the lumen positive, and this voltage drives Mg2+ and Ca2+ through the paracellular path. The proximal tubule reabsorbs about two thirds of filtered sodium and water and nearly all glucose and amino acids, using Na+/H+ exchange and sodium cotransporters. Ischemic injury to these segments explains the high fractional excretion of sodium in acute tubular necrosis.
whyNot: The thick ascending limb is impermeable to water, so there is no solvent drag in this segment.
Na+/H+ exchange drives bicarbonate reabsorption in the proximal tubule. It does not create the voltage that pulls Mg2+ through the paracellular path.
This exchanger moves calcium across distal convoluted tubule cells under PTH control. It does not drive paracellular Mg2+ movement.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains his low urine output during the first days of his illness?
options: Excess ADH from the posterior pituitary
approach: Ischemia kills cells in the straight proximal tubule and the medullary thick ascending limb.
Dead cells detach, form casts, and plug the tubules, raising intratubular pressure and lowering GFR.
Filtrate also leaks back through the bare basement membrane, further reducing urine flow.
questions.why: In ischemic acute tubular necrosis, the energy-hungry straight proximal tubule and medullary thick ascending limb are injured first. Injured cells lose polarity and detach. They clump with Tamm-Horsfall protein into muddy brown granular casts that block the tubules. The obstruction raises tubular pressure and lowers net filtration, and filtrate leaks back through the denuded basement membrane. Afferent vasoconstriction lowers GFR further. Because the tubules cannot reabsorb sodium or concentrate urine, FENa is above 2% and urine osmolality is near 300 mOsm/kg.
whyNot: Immune complexes cause glomerulonephritis with RBC casts and hematuria. His sediment shows granular casts and tubular cells.
Postrenal obstruction would cause hydronephrosis. His granular casts and high FENa point to tubular injury.
Correct.
Excess ADH would make concentrated urine. His urine osmolality of 310 mOsm/kg shows he cannot concentrate.

dx: Rhabdomyolysis-induced acute tubular necrosis after a crush injury with pelvic fracture
case: A 29-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after being pinned under a collapsed wall for 6 hours. His temperature is 36.4 °C (97.5 °F), pulse is 118/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 102/64 mm Hg. Both thighs are swollen and tender. Pelvic radiographs show fractures of the pubic rami. There is blood at the urethral meatus, and rectal examination shows a high-riding prostate. Serum creatine kinase is 52,000 U/L (40 to 200), potassium is 6.1 mEq/L (3.5 to 5.0), and creatinine is 2.6 mg/dL (0.7 to 1.3). A suprapubic catheter drains dark brown urine. Diagnosis: rhabdomyolysis with acute tubular necrosis.

questions.stem: Which of the following urinalysis results is most likely?
options: Negative dipstick for blood with many RBCs
Many dysmorphic RBCs with RBC casts
Positive dipstick for blood with few RBCs
Positive leukocyte esterase with WBC casts
approach: Crush injury and very high creatine kinase mean muscle breakdown releases myoglobin.
Myoglobin is filtered and contains heme, which turns the dipstick blood pad positive.
Microscopy finds few or no red cells, because the heme is not inside red cells.
questions.why: The dipstick blood pad detects the peroxidase-like activity of heme. Myoglobin from muscle breakdown and free hemoglobin from intravascular hemolysis both turn it positive, but microscopy shows few RBCs. Myoglobin injures tubules by direct heme toxicity and oxidant stress, by forming casts, and by causing vasoconstriction. Other nephrotoxic causes of acute tubular necrosis include aminoglycosides, iodinated contrast, cisplatin, and ethylene glycol.
whyNot: The dipstick reacts with the heme in intact red cells, so many RBCs would also give a positive dipstick.
Dysmorphic RBCs and RBC casts mean glomerulonephritis, which bleeds through the glomerulus.
Correct.
WBC casts point to pyelonephritis or interstitial nephritis, not pigment injury.

questions.stem: A urethral catheter was not passed because of the findings at the meatus and on rectal examination. Which of the following parts of the urethra is most likely injured?
options: Spongy urethra in the bulb of the penis
Penile urethra distal to the bulb
Intramural urethra at the bladder neck
approach: Pelvic fracture with blood at the meatus and a high-riding prostate means the urethra has been torn.
The membranous urethra passes through the fixed urogenital diaphragm just below the prostate.
Shearing forces tear it there, and the prostate is displaced upward.
questions.why: The male urethra has prostatic, membranous, and spongy parts. The membranous urethra is short and thin and passes through the external urethral sphincter, held in place by the perineal membrane. In pelvic fracture, the prostate and bladder move while the membranous urethra stays fixed, so it tears at that junction. Urine then leaks into the deep pelvis. A straddle injury instead crushes the bulbous spongy urethra against the pubic arch, and urine collects in the superficial perineal pouch and spreads into the scrotum and abdominal wall.
whyNot: The bulbous spongy urethra is injured by straddle injuries, which crush it against the pubic arch. Urine and blood then spread under the superficial perineal fascia.
The pendulous penile urethra is injured by direct penile trauma or instrumentation, not by pelvic fracture.
Bladder neck injury from pelvic fracture is uncommon in adults, and it would not explain a high-riding prostate.
Correct.

questions.stem: He receives 9 L of 0.9% saline over 24 hours. Laboratory studies then show sodium 141 mEq/L (136 to 145), chloride 115 mEq/L (98 to 106), and bicarbonate 16 mEq/L (22 to 28). The normal anion gap is 8 to 12 mEq/L. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his acidosis at this point?
approach: Calculate the anion gap: 141 - (115 + 16) = 10 mEq/L, which is normal.
A normal gap acidosis means bicarbonate was lost or replaced by chloride, not that an unmeasured acid was added.
Saline has much more chloride than plasma and dilutes bicarbonate, causing a hyperchloremic acidosis.
questions.why: The anion gap is sodium minus chloride plus bicarbonate, normally about 8 to 12 mEq/L. A high gap means an unmeasured acid anion was added: lactate, ketoacids, uremic anions, or toxins such as methanol, ethylene glycol, and salicylate. A normal gap acidosis has high chloride. It comes from bicarbonate loss in diarrhea or renal tubular acidosis, or from large amounts of chloride-rich 0.9% saline. Saline contains 154 mEq/L of chloride and no bicarbonate.
whyNot: Correct.
Lactic acidosis adds an unmeasured anion and raises the anion gap. His gap is normal.
Retained sulfate, phosphate, and urate in kidney failure raise the anion gap. His gap is normal.
Ketoacids are unmeasured anions that raise the anion gap. His gap is normal.

questions.stem: Twelve days later his urine output rises to 4.5 L/day while his creatinine begins to fall. Which of the following electrolyte problems is most likely during this phase of his illness?
approach: Identify the phase: rising urine output with falling creatinine is the recovery phase.
GFR is returning, but the new tubular cells cannot yet reabsorb solutes well.
Large volumes of dilute urine carry away potassium and sodium.
questions.why: Acute tubular necrosis has three phases. Initiation is the period of injury. Maintenance is oliguric, with retention of potassium, H+, phosphate, and water, so hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, and volume overload are the dangers. Recovery begins as tubular cells regrow. GFR returns before reabsorption does, so urine output rises sharply and potassium, sodium, and water are lost. Hypokalemia and volume depletion are the main risks in this polyuric phase.
whyNot: Hyperkalemia belongs to the oliguric maintenance phase, when potassium cannot be excreted. In the polyuric phase potassium is lost.
Correct.
Phosphate retention belongs to the oliguric phase, especially with muscle breakdown. Recovery tubules lose solutes rather than retain them.
Retention of magnesium occurs when GFR is very low. In the polyuric phase, magnesium is wasted rather than retained.

dx: Ethylene glycol poisoning with acute tubular necrosis
case: A 41-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 10 hours after drinking an unknown amount of antifreeze in a suicide attempt. She is confused. Her temperature is 36.8 °C (98.2 °F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 28/min and deep, and blood pressure is 136/84 mm Hg. Laboratory studies show sodium 140 mEq/L (136 to 145), chloride 102 mEq/L (98 to 106), bicarbonate 8 mEq/L (22 to 28), glucose 90 mg/dL (70 to 99), urea nitrogen 14 mg/dL (7 to 20), and creatinine 2.4 mg/dL (0.6 to 1.1). Measured serum osmolality is 322 mOsm/kg (275 to 295), and the calculated osmolality is 290 mOsm/kg. Blood ethanol is undetectable. Diagnosis: ethylene glycol poisoning with acute tubular necrosis.

questions.stem: Which of the following casts is most likely to be seen on microscopy of her urine sediment?
options: Fatty casts with oval fat bodies
approach: Her kidney injury is acute tubular necrosis.
Casts take the shape of the tubule and carry whatever was inside it.
Dead tubular cells breaking down inside casts give muddy brown granular casts.
questions.why: The type of cast tells where the kidney is injured. RBC casts and dysmorphic RBCs mean glomerulonephritis. WBC casts mean pyelonephritis or interstitial nephritis. Muddy brown granular casts made of dead tubular cells mean acute tubular necrosis. Fatty casts mean nephrotic syndrome, and broad waxy casts mean chronic kidney disease. Hyaline casts, made of Tamm-Horsfall protein alone, are nonspecific and are often seen in concentrated urine.
whyNot: RBC casts form when red cells cross a damaged glomerulus. They mark glomerulonephritis.
Correct.
WBC casts mark inflammation in the interstitium, as in pyelonephritis or interstitial nephritis.
Fatty casts and oval fat bodies come from lipid leaking through a damaged glomerulus. They mark nephrotic syndrome.

topics: Urine sediment in acute kidney injury

questions.stem: Measurements over the next few hours, before treatment, show her osmolal gap falling while her anion gap rises. Which of the following processes best explains this change?
options: Renal excretion of unchanged ethylene glycol
Hepatic glucuronide conjugation of the toxin
approach: Unmetabolized ethylene glycol is an uncharged, osmotically active molecule, so it causes the osmolal gap.
NAD+-dependent alcohol dehydrogenase starts its conversion to glycoaldehyde, then glycolic, glyoxylic, and oxalic acids.
As parent alcohol turns into acids, the osmolal gap falls and the anion gap rises.
questions.why: Ethylene glycol itself is not very toxic, but it adds unmeasured osmoles, which explains the early osmolal gap. Alcohol dehydrogenase, using NAD+, starts its oxidation to glycoaldehyde, which aldehyde dehydrogenase turns into glycolic acid. Glycolic acid causes most of the acidosis. Further metabolism produces oxalic acid, which binds calcium to form calcium oxalate crystals that injure tubules. Fomepizole and ethanol block alcohol dehydrogenase and stop toxic acids from forming.
whyNot: Correct.
Excretion would lower the osmolal gap, but it would not create new acids. The anion gap would not rise.
Glucuronidation is not the main route for ethylene glycol and would not make the organic acids that raise the anion gap.
She is not hypotensive. Lactate would raise the anion gap but would not lower the osmolal gap.

questions.stem: Which of the following crystals is most likely to be found in her urine?
approach: Identify ethylene glycol as a nephrotoxic cause of acute tubular necrosis.
Its end product, oxalic acid, binds calcium.
Calcium oxalate crystals, often needle-shaped or envelope-shaped, appear in urine and lodge in tubules.
questions.why: Ethylene glycol is a nephrotoxic cause of acute tubular necrosis. Oxalate from its breakdown binds calcium and forms calcium oxalate crystals that deposit in proximal tubule cells and lumens. Glycolic acid and glycoaldehyde also injure tubular cells directly. Binding of calcium by oxalate can lower serum calcium. Other nephrotoxic causes of acute tubular necrosis include aminoglycosides, iodinated contrast, cisplatin, and myoglobin or hemoglobin pigment.
whyNot: Struvite crystals form in alkaline urine infected by urease-producing bacteria such as Proteus.
Uric acid crystals form in acidic urine with high uric acid, as in gout or tumor lysis syndrome.
Cystine crystals are hexagonal and form in cystinuria, an inherited defect in dibasic amino acid reabsorption.
Correct.

questions.stem: Her anion gap is 30 mEq/L (8 to 12), and her osmolal gap is 32 mOsm/kg (less than 10). Which of the following conditions would also be expected to produce both a high anion gap and a high osmolal gap?
approach: Confirm the anion gap: 140 - (102 + 8) = 30 mEq/L, which is high.
A high osmolal gap means an unmeasured, osmotically active substance, usually a toxic alcohol.
A toxic alcohol that is metabolized to an acid gives both gaps: ethylene glycol or methanol.
questions.why: The anion gap is sodium minus chloride plus bicarbonate. High anion gap acidosis comes from lactic acidosis, ketoacidosis, uremia, methanol, ethylene glycol, and salicylates. Normal anion gap acidosis comes from diarrhea and renal tubular acidosis. A high osmolal gap means an unmeasured osmole such as a toxic alcohol. Methanol, like ethylene glycol, is converted by alcohol dehydrogenase to an acid (formic acid), so both gaps rise. Methanol damages the retina and optic nerve, while ethylene glycol damages the kidney.
whyNot: Isopropyl alcohol raises the osmolal gap, but it is metabolized to acetone, which is not an acid. The anion gap stays normal.
Salicylates cause a high anion gap acidosis, often with respiratory alkalosis, but do not cause a significant osmolal gap.
Correct.
Diarrhea removes bicarbonate and causes a normal anion gap, hyperchloremic acidosis without an osmolal gap.
